entries.c553f86df89488de87e2edb73ae059b7cb5eaf0c: <div sID="gen20129" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Amos.4" sID="Amos.4"/> <div eID="gen20129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20130" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20131" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. The oppressors in Israel are threatened for their oppression of the poor, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.1-Amos.4.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The idolaters in Israel, being joined to idols, are given up to their own heart's lusts, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.4-Amos.4.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. III. All the sins of Israel are aggravated from their incorrigibleness in them, and their refusal to return and reform, notwithstanding the various rebukes of Providence which they had been under, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.6-Amos.4.11">ver. 6-11</reference>. IV. They are invited yet at length to humble themselves before God, since it is impossible for them to make their part good against him, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.12-Amos.4.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>.
entries.39ec9e70fe626da8e75c1ca42546768e160775cd: <div eID="gen20131" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20130" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings against Oppressors; Punishment of Proud Oppressors. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20132" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear this word, ye kine of Bashan, that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the mountain of Samaria, which oppress the poor, which crush the needy, which say to their masters, Bring, and let us drink. <hi type="super">2</hi> The Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> hath sworn by his holiness, that, lo, the days shall come upon you, that he will take you away with hooks, and your posterity with fish-hooks. <hi type="super">3</hi> And ye shall go out at the breaches, every <hi type="italic">cow at that which is</hi> before her; and ye shall cast <hi type="italic">them</hi> into the palace, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">4</hi> Come to Bethel, and transgress; at Gilgal multiply transgression; and bring your sacrifices every morning, <hi type="italic">and</hi> your tithes after three years: <hi type="super">5</hi> And offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving with leaven, and proclaim <hi type="italic">and</hi> publish the free offerings: for this liketh you, O ye children of Israel, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen20132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20133" type="x-p"/> It is here foretold, in the name of God, that oppressors shall be humbled and idolaters shall be hardened. <div eID="gen20133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20134" type="x-p"/> I. That proud oppressors shall be humbled for their oppressions: for <hi type="italic">he that does wrong shall receive according to the wrong that he has done.</hi> Now observe, <div eID="gen20134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20135" type="x-p"/> 1. How their sin is described, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.1">v. 1</reference>. They are compared to the <hi type="italic">kine of Bashan,</hi> which were a breed of cattle very large and strong, especially if, though bred there, they were fed upon <hi type="italic">the mountain of Samaria,</hi> where the pastures were extraordinarily fat. Amos had been a herdsman, and he speaks in a dialect of his calling, comparing the rich and great men, that lived in luxury and wantonness, to the <hi type="italic">kine of Bashan,</hi> which were wanton and unruly, would not be kept within the bounds of their own pasture, But broke through the hedges, broke down all the fences, and trespassed upon the neighboring grounds; and not only so, but pushed and gored the smaller cattle that were not a match for them. Those that had their summer-houses upon the mountains of Samaria when they went thither for fresh air were as mischievous as the kine upon the mountains of Bashan and as injurious to those about them. (1.) They oppress the poor and needy themselves; they <hi type="italic">crush</hi> them, to squeeze something to themselves out of them. They took advantage of their poverty, and necessity, and inability to help themselves, to make them poorer and more necessitous than they were. They made use of their power as judges and magistrates for the invading of men's rights and properties, the poor not excepted; for they made no conscience of robbing even the hospital. (2.) They are in confederacy with those that do so. They <hi type="italic">say to their masters</hi> (to the masters of the poor, that abuse them and violently take from them what they have, when they ought to relieve them), "<hi type="italic">Bring, and let us drink;</hi> let us feast with you upon the gains of our oppression, and then we will protect you, and stand by you in it, and reject the appeals of the poor against you." Note, What is got by extortion is commonly made use of as <hi type="italic">provisions for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof;</hi> and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> men are tyrants to the poor because they are slaves to their appetites. <hi type="italic">Bring, and let us drink,</hi> is the language of those that <hi type="italic">crush the needy,</hi> as if the <hi type="italic">tears of the oppressed,</hi> mingled with their wine, made it drink the better. And by their associations for drinking and reveling, and an excess of riot, they strengthen their combinations for persecution and oppression, and harden the hearts of one another in it. <div eID="gen20135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20136" type="x-p"/> 2. How their punishment is described, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.2-Amos.4.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. God will <hi type="italic">take them away with hooks, and their posterity with fish-hooks;</hi> he will send the Assyrian army upon them, that shall make a prey of them, shall not only enclose the body of the nation in their net, but shall angle for particular persons, and take them prisoners and captives as with hooks and fish-hooks, shall draw them out of their own land as fish are drawn out of the water, which is their element, them and their children with them, or, They in their day shall be drawn out by one victorious enemy, and their posterity in their day by another, so that by a succession of destroying judgments they shall at length be wholly extirpated. These <hi type="italic">kine of Bashan</hi> thought they could no more be drawn out with a hook and a cord than the Leviathan can, <reference osisRef="Job.41.1-Job.41.2">Job xli. 1, 2</reference>. But God will make them know that he has a <hi type="italic">hook for their nose</hi> and a <hi type="italic">bridle for their jaws,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Isa. xxxvii. 29</reference>. The enemy shall take them away as easily as the fisherman takes away the little fish, and shall make it their sport and recreation. When the enemy has made himself master of Samaria, then, (1.) Some shall attempt to escape by flight: <hi type="italic">You shall go out at the breaches</hi> made in the wall of the city, <hi type="italic">every cow at that which is before her,</hi> to shift for her own safety, and make the best of her way; and now the unruly kine of Bashan are tamed, and are themselves crushed, as they crushed the poor and needy. Note, Those to whom God has given a good pasture, if they are wanton in it, will justly be turned out of it; and those who will not be kept within the hedge of God's precept forfeit the benefit of the hedge of God's protection, and will be forced in vain to flee through the breaches they have themselves fearfully made in that hedge. (2.) Others shall think to shelter themselves, or at least their best effects, in the palace, because it is a castle well fortified and a garrison well manned: <hi type="italic">You shall throw yourselves</hi> (so some read it), or <hi type="italic">throw them</hi> (that is, your posterity, your children, or whatever is dear to you), <hi type="italic">into the palace,</hi> where the enemy will find it ready to be seized. Note, What is got by oppression cannot long be enjoyed with satisfaction. <div eID="gen20136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20137" type="x-p"/> 3. How their sentence to this punishment is ratified: <hi type="italic">The Lord God has sworn it by his holiness.</hi> He had often said it, and they regarded it not; they thought God and his prophets did but jest with them; therefore he <hi type="italic">swears</hi> it <hi type="italic">in his wrath,</hi> and what he has sworn he will not revoke. He swears by <hi type="italic">his holiness,</hi> that attribute of his which is so much his glory, and which is so much glorified in the punishment of wicked people; for, as sure as God is a holy God, those that <hi type="italic">plough iniquity and sow wickedness shall reap the same.</hi> <div eID="gen20137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20138" type="x-p"/> II. That obstinate idolaters shall be hardened in their idolatries (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.4-Amos.4.5">v. 4, 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Come to Bethel, and transgress.</hi> It is spoken ironically: "Do so; take your course; <hi type="italic">multiply</hi> your <hi type="italic">transgressions</hi> by multiplying your sacrifices, <hi type="italic">for this liketh you;</hi> but what will you do in the end hereof?" Here we see, 1. How intent they were upon the service of their idols, and how willing they were to be at cost upon them; they <hi type="italic">brought their sacrifices,</hi> and their <hi type="italic">tithes,</hi> and their <hi type="italic">free-will offerings,</hi> hoping that therein they should be accepted of God, but it was all an abomination to him. The profuseness of idolaters in the service of their false gods may shame our strait-handedness in the service of the true and living God. 2. How they mimicked God's institutions. They had their <hi type="italic">daily sacrifice</hi> at the altar of Bethel, as God had at his altar; they had their <hi type="italic">thank-offerings</hi> as God had, only they allowed <hi type="italic">leaven</hi> in them, which God had forbidden, because their priests did not like to have the bread to heavy and tasteless as it would be if it had not leaven in it, for something to ferment it. Holy bread would not serve them, unless it were pleasant bread. 3. How well pleased they were with these services themselves: <hi type="italic">This liketh you, O you children of Israel! So you love.</hi> What was their own invention they were fond of and wedded to, and thought it must be pleasing to God because it was agreeable to their own fancy. 4. How they upbraided with it: "<hi type="italic">Come to Bethel, to Gilgal; bring the sacrifices</hi> and <hi type="italic">tithes</hi> yourselves; <hi type="italic">proclaim</hi> and <hi type="italic">publish</hi> to the nation the <hi type="italic">free-offerings,</hi> pressing them to bring in abundance of such; <hi type="italic">go on</hi> in this way;" that is, (1.) "It is plain that you are resolved to do it, whatever God and conscience say to the contrary." (2.) "Your prophets shall let you alone in it, and not admonish you as they have done, for it is to no purpose. <hi type="italic">Let no man strive nor rebuke his neighbour.</hi>" (3.) "Your foolish hearts shall be more and more darkened and besotted, and you shall be quite <hi type="italic">given up to</hi> these <hi type="italic">strong delusions, to believe a lie.</hi>" (4.) "What will you get by it? <hi type="italic">Come to Bethel</hi> and <hi type="italic">multiply your sacrifices,</hi> and see what the better you will be, what returns you will have to your sacrifices, what stead they will stand you in in the day of distress. <hi type="italic">You shall be ashamed of Bethel your confidence,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.48.13">Jer. xlviii. 13</reference>. (5.) "<hi type="italic">Come, and transgress,</hi> come, and <hi type="italic">multiply your transgression,</hi> that you may <hi type="italic">fill up the measure</hi> of your iniquity and be ripened for ruin." Thus Christ said to Judas, <hi type="italic">What thou doest do quickly;</hi> and to the Jews, <hi type="italic">Fill you up the measure of your fathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.32">Matt. xxiii. 32</reference>.
entries.325bd0e52c371e1dbaa8c7698d2e112d219e4ebf: <div eID="gen20138" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Incorrigibleness of Israel; Judgments Called to Remembrance; Greater Judgments Threatened. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  790.)</title> <div sID="gen20139" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And I also have given you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and want of bread in all your places: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> And also I have withholden the rain from you, when <hi type="italic">there were</hi> yet three months to the harvest: and I caused it to rain upon one city, and caused it not to rain upon another city: one piece was rained upon, and the piece whereupon it rained not withered. <hi type="super">8</hi> So two <hi type="italic">or</hi> three cities wandered unto one city, to drink water; but they were not satisfied: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> I have smitten you with blasting and mildew: when your gardens and your vineyards and your fig trees and your olive trees increased, the palmer-worm devoured <hi type="italic">them:</hi> yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">10</hi> I have sent among you the pestilence after the manner of Egypt: your young men have I slain with the sword, and have taken away your horses; and I have made the stink of your camps to come up unto your nostrils: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">11</hi> I have overthrown <hi type="italic">some</hi> of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">12</hi> Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: <hi type="italic">and</hi> because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel. <hi type="super">13</hi> For, lo, he that formeth the mountains, and createth the wind, and declareth unto man what <hi type="italic">is</hi> his thought, that maketh the morning darkness, and treadeth upon the high places of the earth, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , The God of hosts, <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name. <div eID="gen20139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20140" type="x-p"/> Here, I. God complains of his people's incorrigibleness under the judgments which he had brought upon them in order to their humiliation and reformation. He had by several tokens intimated to them his displeasure, with this design, that they might by repentance make their peace with him; but it had not that effect. <div eID="gen20140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20141" type="x-p"/> 1. It is five times repeated in these verses, as the burden of the charge, "<hi type="italic">Yet have you not returned unto me, saith the Lord;</hi> you have been several times corrected, but in vain; you are not reclaimed, there is no sign of amendment. You have been sent for by one messenger after another, but you have not come back, you have not come home." (1.) This intimates that that which God designed in all his providential rebukes was to reduce them to their allegiance, to influence them to return to him. (2.) That, if they had returned to their God, they would have been accepted, he would have bidden them welcome, and the troubles they were in would have been removed. (3.) That the reason why God sent further troubles was because former troubles had not done the work, otherwise it is <hi type="italic">no pleasure to the Almighty that he should afflict.</hi> (4.) That God was grieved at their obstinacy, and took it unkindly that they should force him to do that which he did so unwillingly: "<hi type="italic">You have not returned to me</hi> from whom you have revolted, <hi type="italic">to me</hi> with whom you are in covenant, <hi type="italic">to me</hi> who stands ready to receive you, <hi type="italic">to me</hi> who have so often called you." Now, <div eID="gen20141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20142" type="x-p"/> 2. To aggravate their incorrigibleness, and to justify himself in inflicting greater judgments, he recounts the less judgments with which he had tried to bring them to repentance. <div eID="gen20142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20143" type="x-p"/> (1.) There had sometimes been a scarcity of provisions, though there was no visible cause of it (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have given you cleanness of teeth in all your cities,</hi> for you had no meat to chew, whereby your teeth might be fouled," especially no flesh, which dirties the teeth. Or, <hi type="italic">I have given you emptiness of teeth,</hi> nothing to fill your mouths with. "<hi type="italic">Bread,</hi> the staff of life, has been wanting, for you have <hi type="italic">sown much</hi> and <hi type="italic">brought in little,</hi>" as <reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">Hag. i. 9</reference>. Some think this refers to that <hi type="italic">seven years' famine</hi> that was in Elisha's time, which we read of <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.1">2 Kings viii. 1</reference>. Now when God thus <hi type="italic">took away their corn in the season thereof,</hi> because they had prepared it for Baal, they should have said, We will <hi type="italic">go and return to our first husband,</hi> having paid dearly for leaving him; but it had not that effect. <hi type="italic">They have not returned to me,</hi> saith the Lord. <div eID="gen20143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20144" type="x-p"/> (2.) Sometimes they had wanted rain, and then of course they wanted the fruits of the earth. This evil was of the Lord: <hi type="italic">I have withholden the rain from you.</hi> God has the key of the clouds, and, if he shut up, who can open? <reference osisRef="Amos.4.7">v. 7</reference>. The rain was withheld <hi type="italic">when there were yet three months to the harvest,</hi> at the time when they used to have it, and therefore the withholding of it was an extraordinary thing, and, if the course of nature was altered, they must therein own the hand of the God of nature; and it was at a time when they most needed it, and therefore the want of it was a very sore judgment, and blasted their expectations of a crop at harvest. And one circumstance which made this very remarkable was that when there were some places that wanted rain, and withered for want of it, there were other places near adjoining that had it in abundance. God <hi type="italic">caused it to rain upon one city, and not upon another,</hi> in the same country; nay, he caused it to rain <hi type="italic">upon one field,</hi> one <hi type="italic">piece</hi> of a field, and it was thereby made fruitful and flourishing, but on the next field, on the other side of the hedge, nay, on another part of the same field, <hi type="italic">it rained not</hi> at all, and it was so long without rain that all the products of it <hi type="italic">withered.</hi> No doubt this was literally true, and there were many instances of it which were generally taken notice of. Now, [1.] By this it appeared that the withholding of the rain was not casual, but by a divine direction and disposal, and that the cloud which waters the earth is <hi type="italic">turned round about by the counsels of God, to do whatsoever he commands it, whether for correction, or for his land, or for his mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.37.12-Job.37.18">Job xxxvii. 12-18</reference>. Rain does not go by planets (as common people speak), but as God sends it by his winds. [2.] We have reason to think that those cities on which it rained not were the most infamous for wickedness, such as Bethel and Gilgal (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.4">v. 4</reference>), and that those on which it rained were such as retained something of religion and virtue among them. And so in the town-fields it rained or rained not, upon the piece, according as the owner was; for we are sure <hi type="italic">the curse of the Lord is in the house,</hi> and upon the ground, <hi type="italic">of the wicked, but he blesses the habitation of the just,</hi> and his field is a <hi type="italic">field that the Lord has blessed.</hi> [3.] It would be the greater grief and vexation to those whose fields withered for want of rain to see their neighbours' fields well watered and flourishing. <hi type="italic">My servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.13">Isa. lxv. 13</reference>. The <hi type="italic">wicked shall see it, and be grieved.</hi> Probably those that were oppressed were rained upon, and so they recovered their losses, while the oppressors withered, and so lost their gains. [4.] Yet, as to the nation in general, it was a mixture of mercy with the judgment, and, consequently, strengthened the call to repentance and reformation, and encouraged them to hope for all mercy, in their returns to God, since there was so much mercy even in God's rebukes of them. But, because they did not make good use of this gracious allay to the extremity of the judgment, they had not the benefit of it, which otherwise they might have had, for (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.8">v. 8</reference>) <hi type="italic">two or three cities wandered</hi> at uncertainty, as beggars, <hi type="italic">unto one city, to drink water,</hi> and, if possible, to have some to carry home with them, but <hi type="italic">they were not satisfied;</hi> it was but here and there one city that had water, while many wanted, and then it was not, as usual, <hi type="italic">Usus communis aquarum—Water is free to all.</hi> Those that had it had occasion for it, or knew not how soon they might, and therefore could afford but little to those that wanted, saying, <hi type="italic">Lest there be not enough for us and you.</hi> Those that came <hi type="italic">drank water,</hi> but <hi type="italic">they were not satisfied,</hi> because they drank it <hi type="italic">by measure, and with astonishment;</hi> and those that <hi type="italic">drink of this water shall thirst again,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.13">John iv. 13</reference>. They were not satisfied, because their desires were greedy, and what they had God did not bless to them, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">Hag. i. 6</reference>. And now, one would think, when they met with all this disappointment, they should have considered their ways and repented; but it had not that effect: "<hi type="italic">Yet have you not returned to me,</hi> no, not so much as to pray in a right manner for the former and latter rain," <reference osisRef="Zech.10.1">Zech. x. 1</reference>. See the folly of carnal hearts; they will wander from city to city, from one creature to another, in pursuit of satisfaction, and still they miss of it; they <hi type="italic">labour for that which satisfies not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa. lv. 2</reference>), and yet, after all, they <hi type="italic">will not return to God,</hi> will not incline their ear to him in whom they might have satisfaction. The preaching of the gospel is as rain; God sometimes blesses one place with it more than another; some countries, some cities, are, like Gideon's fleece, wet with this dew, while the ground about is dry; all withers where this rain is wanting. But it were well if people were but as wise for their souls as they are for their bodies, and, when they have not this rain near them, would go and seek it where it is to be had; and, if they seek aright, they shall not seek in vain. <div eID="gen20144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20145" type="x-p"/> (3.) Sometimes the fruits of their ground were eaten up by caterpillars, or blasted with mildew, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.9">v. 9</reference>. Heaven and earth are armed against those who have made God their enemy. When God pleased, that is, when he was displeased, [1.] They suffered by a malignant air, the influence of which, either too hot or too cold, blasted their fruits, with a force that could be neither discerned nor resisted, and against which there was no defence. [2.] They suffered by malignant animals. Their <hi type="italic">vineyards</hi> and <hi type="italic">gardens</hi> yielded their increase in great abundance, so did their <hi type="italic">fig-trees</hi> and <hi type="italic">olive-trees;</hi> but the <hi type="italic">palmer-worm devoured them</hi> before the fruits were ripe, and fit to be gathered in. This was either the same judgment with that which we read of <reference osisRef="Joel.1.4-Joel.1.6">Joel i. 4-6</reference>, or a less judgment of the same nature, sent before to give warning of that. But they did not take warning: <hi type="italic">Yet have you not returned unto me.</hi> <div eID="gen20145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20146" type="x-p"/> (4.) Sometimes the plague had raged among them, and the sword of war had cut off multitudes, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.10">v. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">The pestilence</hi> is God's messenger; this he <hi type="italic">sent among</hi> them, with directions whom to strike dead, and it was done. It was a <hi type="italic">pestilence after the manner of Egypt;</hi> deaths were scattered among them by the hand of a <hi type="italic">destroying angel at midnight.</hi> And perhaps this pestilence, as that of Egypt, fastened upon the first-born. <hi type="italic">In the way of Egypt</hi> (so the margin); when they were making their escape to Egypt, or going thither to seek for aid, the pestilence seized them by the way and stopped their journey. The sword of war is likewise <hi type="italic">the sword of the Lord;</hi> this was drawn among them with commission; and then it <hi type="italic">slew their young men,</hi> the strength of the present generation and the seed of the next. God says, <hi type="italic">I have slain them;</hi> he avows the execution. <hi type="italic">The slain of the Lord are many.</hi> The enemy <hi type="italic">took away their horses,</hi> and converted them to their own use; and the dead carcases of those that were slain either with sword or pestilence were so many, and for want of surviving friends were left so long unburied, that the <hi type="italic">stench of their camps came up into their nostrils,</hi> and was both noisome and dangerous, and might put them in mind of the offensiveness of their sin to God. And yet this did not prevail to humble and reclaim them: <hi type="italic">You have not returned to</hi> him that smites you. Such a rueful woeful sight as this prevailed not to make them religious. <div eID="gen20146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20147" type="x-p"/> (5.) In these and other judgments some were remarkably cut off, and made monuments of justice, others were remarkably spared, and made monuments of mercy, the setting of which the one over against the other one would have thought likely to work upon them, but it had not its effect, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.11">v. 11</reference>. [1.] Some were quite ruined, their families destroyed, and themselves in them: <hi type="italic">I have overthrown some of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.</hi> Perhaps they were consumed with lightning, as Sodom was, or the houses were, in some other way, burnt to the ground, and the inhabitants in them. Sodom and Gomorrah are said to be <hi type="italic">condemned with an overthrow, and so made an example,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.6">2 Pet. ii. 6</reference>. God had threatened to destroy the whole land with such an overthrow as that of Sodom, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">Deut. xxix. 23</reference>. But he began with some particular places first, to give them warning, or perhaps with some particular persons, whose <hi type="italic">sins went beforehand to judgment.</hi> [2.] Others very narrowly escaped: "You <hi type="italic">were</hi> many of you as a <hi type="italic">firebrand plucked out of the burning,</hi> like Lot out of Sodom, when the fire had already kindled upon you; and yet you hate sin never the more for the danger it has brought you to, nor love God ever the more for the deliverance he wrought for you. You that have been so signally delivered, and in such a distinguishing way, <hi type="italic">have not returned unto me.</hi>" <div eID="gen20147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20148" type="x-p"/> II. God, in the close, calls upon his people, now at length, in this their day, to understand the things that belong to their peace, before they were hidden from their eyes, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.12-Amos.4.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen20148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20149" type="x-p"/> 1. How God threatens them with sorer judgments than any they had yet been under: "Therefore, seeing you have not been wrought upon by correction hitherto, <hi type="italic">thus will I do unto thee, O Israel!</hi>" He does not say how he will do, but it shall be something worse than had come yet, <reference osisRef="John.5.14">John v. 14</reference>. Or, "<hi type="italic">Thus I will</hi> go on to <hi type="italic">do unto thee,</hi> following one judgment with another, like the plagues of Egypt, till I have made a full end." Nothing but reformation will prevent the ruin of a sinful people. If they turn not to him, his anger is not <hi type="italic">turned away,</hi> but <hi type="italic">his hand is stretched out still. I will punish you yet seven times more, if you will not be reformed;</hi> so it was written in the law, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.23-Lev.26.24">Lev. xxvi. 23, 24</reference>. <div eID="gen20149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20150" type="x-p"/> 2. How he awakens them therefore to think of making their peace with God: "<hi type="italic">Seeing I will do this unto thee,</hi> and there is no remedy, <hi type="italic">prepare to meet they God, O Israel!</hi>" that is, (1.) "Consider how unable thou art to meet him as a combatant." Some make it to be spoken by way of irony or challenge: "Prepare to meet God, who is coming forth to contend with thee. What armour of proof canst thou put on? What courage canst thou steel thyself with? Alas! it is but putting <hi type="italic">briers and thorns</hi> before a consuming fire, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4-Isa.27.5">Isa. xxvii. 4, 5</reference>. Art thou able with less than 10,000 to meet him that comes forth against thee with more than 20,000?" <reference osisRef="Luke.14.31">Luke xiv. 31</reference>. (2.) "Resolve therefore to meet him as a penitent, as a humble suppliant, to meet him as <hi type="italic">thy God,</hi> in covenant with thee, to submit, and stand it out no longer." We must prepare to <hi type="italic">meet God in the way of his judgments</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.8">Isa. xxvi. 8</reference>), to <hi type="italic">take hold on his strength, that we may make peace.</hi> Note, Since we cannot flee from God we are concerned to prepare to meet him; and therefore he gives us warning, that we may prepare. When we are to meet him in his ordinances we must prepare to meet him, prepare to seek him. <div eID="gen20150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20151" type="x-p"/> 3. How he sets forth the greatness and power of God as a reason why we should prepare to meet him, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.13">v. 13</reference>. If he be such a God as he is here described to be, it is folly to contend with him, and our duty and interest to make our peace with him; it is good having him our friend and bad having him our enemy. (1.) He <hi type="italic">formed the mountains,</hi> made the earth, the strongest stateliest parts of it, and by the word of his power still upholds it and them. Whatever are the products of the everlasting mountains, he formed them; whatever <hi type="italic">salvation</hi> is <hi type="italic">hoped for from hills and mountains,</hi> he is the founder of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.11-Ps.89.12">Ps. lxxxix. 11, 12</reference>. He that formed the <hi type="italic">great mountains</hi> can <hi type="italic">make them plain,</hi> when they stand in the way of his people's salvation. (2.) He <hi type="italic">creates the wind.</hi> The power of the air is derived from him, and directed by him; he brings the wind out of his treasures, and orders from what point of the compass it shall blow; and he that made it rules it; even <hi type="italic">the winds and the seas obey him.</hi> (3.) He <hi type="italic">declares unto man what is his thought.</hi> He makes known his counsel by his servants the prophets to the children of men, the thought of his justice against impenitent sinners, and the thought of good he thinks towards those that repent. He can also make known, for he perfectly knows, the thought that is in man's heart; he <hi type="italic">understands it afar off,</hi> and in the day of conviction will set the evil thoughts among the other sins of sinners <hi type="italic">in order before them.</hi> (4.) He often <hi type="italic">makes the morning darkness,</hi> by thick clouds overspreading the sky immediately after the sun rose bright and glorious; so when we look for prosperity and joy he can dash our expectations with some unlooked-for calamity. (5.) He <hi type="italic">treads upon the high places of the earth,</hi> is not only higher than the highest, but has dominion over all, tramples upon proud men, and upon the idols that were worshipped in the highest places. (6.) <hi type="italic">Jehovah the God of hosts is his name,</hi> for he has his being of himself, and is the fountain of all being, and all the hosts of heaven and earth are at his command. Let us humble ourselves before this God, prepare to meet him, and give all diligence to make him our God, for happy are the people whose God he is, who have all this power engaged for them.  <chapter eID="Amos.4"/> <div eID="gen20151" type="x-p"/>

entries.97494a3a2fcf13e21694c61b1be4d358cac75502: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12552"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Amos.4.1-Amos.4.13">Am 4:1-13</reference>. Denunciation of Israel's Nobles for Oppression; and of the Whole Nation for Idolatry; and for Their Being Unreformed Even by God's Judgments: Therefore They Must Prepare for the Last and Worst Judgment of All.</title> <div sID="gen23109" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12552"/><hi type="bold">1. kine of Bashan--</hi>fat and wanton cattle such as the rich pasture of Bashan (east of Jordan, between Hermon and Gilead) was famed for (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.14">De 32:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.12">Psa 22:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.18">Eze 39:18</reference>). Figurative for those luxurious nobles mentioned, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.9">Am 3:9</reference>, 10, 12, 15. The feminine, kine, or cows, not bulls, expresses their effeminacy. This accounts for masculine forms in the Hebrew being intermixed with feminine; the latter being figurative, the former the real persons meant.<div eID="gen23109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">say to their masters--</hi>that is, to their king, with whom the princes indulged in potations (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.5">Ho 7:5</reference>), and whom here they importune for more wine. "Bring" is singular, in the Hebrew implying that one "master" alone is meant. <div eID="gen23110" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c691c92fca07ae3baf4e3b08c449e04f278c1b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12553"/><div sID="gen23111" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12553"/><hi type="bold">2. The Lord--</hi>the same Hebrew as "masters" (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.1">Am 4:1</reference>). Israel's nobles say to their master or lord, Bring us drink: but "the Lord" of him and them "hath sworn," &c.<div eID="gen23111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by his holiness--</hi>which binds Him to punish the guilty (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.35">Psa 89:35</reference>).<div eID="gen23112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he will take yon away--</hi>that is God by the instrumentality of the enemy.<div eID="gen23113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with hooks--</hi>literally, "thorns" (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.11">2Ch 33:11</reference>). As fish are taken out of the water by hooks, so the Israelites are to be taken out of their cities by the enemy (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.4">Eze 29:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job 41:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.16">Jr 16:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.15">Ha 1:15</reference>). The image is the more appropriate, as anciently captives were led by their conquerors by a hook made to pass through the nose (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.28">2Ki 19:28</reference>), as is to be seen in the Assyrian remains. <div eID="gen23114" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f141fb6ea8761aeafe8b9faf3e6146abaf9085e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12554"/><div sID="gen23115" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12554"/><hi type="bold">3. go out at the breaches--</hi>namely, of the city walls broken by the enemy.<div eID="gen23115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every cow at that which is before her--</hi>figurative for the once luxurious nobles (compare "kine of Bashan," <reference osisRef="Amos.4.1">Am 4:1</reference>) shall go out each one right before her; not through the gates, but each at the breach before him, not turning to the right or left, apart from one another.<div eID="gen23116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23117" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye shall cast them into the palace--</hi>"them," that is, "your posterity," from <reference osisRef="Amos.4.2">Am 4:2</reference>. You yourselves shall escape through the breaches, after having cast your little children into the palace, so as not to see their destruction, and to escape the more quickly. Rather, "ye shall cast yourselves into the palace," so as to escape from it out of the city [Calvin]. The palace, the scene of the princes' riots (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.10">Am 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.1">4:1</reference>), is to be the scene of their ignominious flight. Compare in the similar case of Jerusalem's capture, the king's escape by way of the palace, through a breach in the wall (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.5">Eze 12:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.12">12</reference>). Gesenius translates, "Ye shall be cast (as captives) into the (enemy's) stronghold"; in this view, the enemy's stronghold is called "palace," in retributive contrast to the "palaces" of Israel's nobles, the store houses of their robberies (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.10">Am 3:10</reference>). <div eID="gen23117" type="x-p"/>
entries.261dd9745613b736d13f0d240eedcc09f0c1baf8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12555"/><div sID="gen23118" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12555"/>4. God gives them up to their self-willed idolatry, that they may see how unable their idols are to save them from their coming calamities. So <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.39">Eze 20:39</reference>.<div eID="gen23118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beth-el--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.3.14">Am 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen23119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gilgal--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Ho 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.15">9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.11">12:11</reference>).<div eID="gen23120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sacrifices every morning--</hi>as commanded in the law (<reference osisRef="Num.28.3">Nu 28:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.28.4">4</reference>). They imitated the letter, while violating by calf-worship the spirit, of the Jerusalem temple-worship.<div eID="gen23121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after three years--</hi>every third year; literally, "after three (years of) days" (that is, the fullest complement of days, or a year); "after three full years." Compare <reference osisRef="Lev.25.20">Le 25:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.17.10">Jud 17:10</reference>, and "the days" for the years, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.2">Joe 1:2</reference>. So a month of days is used for a full month, wanting no day to complete it (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.14">Ge 29:14</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Num.11.20">Nu 11:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.11.21">21</reference>). The Israelites here also kept to the letter of the law in bringing in the tithes of their increase every third year (<reference osisRef="Deut.14.28">De 14:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.26.12">26:12</reference>). <div eID="gen23122" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7cd8c82cb9b19f919169ac073d1a199844f1558: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12556"/><div sID="gen23123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12556"/><hi type="bold">5. offer--</hi>literally, "burn incense"; that is, "offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving with burnt incense and with leavened bread." The frankincense was laid on the meat offering, and taken by the priest from it to burn on the altar (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.1">Le 2:1</reference>, 2, 8-11). Though unleavened cakes were to accompany the peace offering sacrifice of animals, leavened bread was also commanded (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.12">Le 7:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.13">13</reference>), but not as a "meat offering" (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.11">Le 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen23123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this liketh you--</hi>that is, this is what ye like. <div eID="gen23124" type="x-p"/>
entries.151e3fc8604bd927d908af484dcfe38a830ce32c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12557"/><div sID="gen23125" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12557"/>6-11. Jehovah details His several chastisements inflicted with a view to reclaiming them: but adds to each the same sad result, "yet have ye not returned unto Me" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Is 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.3">Jr 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.7.10">Ho 7:10</reference>); the monotonous repetition of the same burden marking their pitiable obstinacy.<div eID="gen23125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cleanness of teeth--</hi>explained by the parallel, "want of bread." The famine alluded to is that mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.1">2Ki 8:1</reference> [Grotius]. Where there is no food to masticate, the teeth are free from uncleanness, but it is the cleanness of want. Compare <reference osisRef="Prov.14.4">Pr 14:4</reference>, "Where no oxen are, the crib is clean." So spiritually, where all is outwardly smooth and clean, it is often because there is no solid religion. Better fighting and fears with real piety, than peace and respectable decorum without spiritual life. <div eID="gen23126" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b0de3e2859bb254f94cd3e8645ec4d686dbae08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12563"/><div sID="gen23140" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12563"/><hi type="bold">12. Therefore--</hi>as all chastisements have failed to make thee "return unto Me."<div eID="gen23140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thus will I do unto thee--</hi>as I have threatened (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.2">Am 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen23141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23142" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prepare to meet thy God--</hi>God is about to inflict the last and worst judgment on thee, the extinction of thy nationality; consider then what preparation thou canst make for encountering Him as thy foe (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.14">Jr 46:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.14.31">Lu 14:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.32">32</reference>). But as that would be madness to think of (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Is 27:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.14">Eze 22:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.31">He 10:31</reference>), see what can be done towards mitigating the severity of the coming judgment, by penitence (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.5">Is 27:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.31">1Co 11:31</reference>). This latter exhortation is followed up in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.4">Am 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">6, 8</reference>, 14, 15. <div eID="gen23142" type="x-p"/>
entries.dedb01d0d952f548d8aa25f36a804f245eeb8a51: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12564"/><div sID="gen23143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12564"/>13. The God whom Israel is to "prepare to meet" (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.12">Am 4:12</reference>) is here described in sublime terms.<div eID="gen23143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wind--</hi>not as the Margin, "spirit." The God with whom thou hast to do is the Omnipotent Maker of things seen, such as the stupendous mountains, and of things too subtle to be seen, though of powerful agency, as the "wind."<div eID="gen23144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">declareth unto man ... his thought--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.139.2">Psa 139:2</reference>). Ye think that your secret thoughts escape My cognizance, but I am the searcher of hearts.<div eID="gen23145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">maketh ... morning darkness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.5.8">Am 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">8:9</reference>). Both literally turning the sunshine into darkness, and figuratively turning the prosperity of the ungodly into sudden adversity (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.12">Psa 73:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.19">18, 19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.13.16">Jr 13:16</reference>).<div eID="gen23146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">treadeth upon ... high places--</hi>God treadeth down the proud of the earth. He subjects to Him all things however high they be (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.3">Mi 1:3</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">De 32:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">33:29</reference>, where the same phrase is used of God's people, elevated by God above every other human height. <chapter eID="Amos.4"/>

entries.d1250a170b074d09c8e1d1677210b9c87388a18b: <div eID="gen34312" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34313" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34314" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34314" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34313" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34315" type="x-p"/> Israel reproved for their oppression, <reference osisRef="Amo.4.1-Amo.4.3">Amo 4:1-3</reference>; idolatry, <reference osisRef="Amo.4.4">Amo 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amo.4.5">Amo 4:5</reference>; and for their impenitence under the chastising hand of God, <reference osisRef="Amo.4.6-Amo.4.11">Amo 4:6-11</reference>. The omniscience and uncontrollable power of God, <reference osisRef="Amo.4.12">Amo 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amo.4.13">Amo 4:13</reference>. <div eID="gen34315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34316" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34317" type="x-p"/> Hear this word, ye kine of Bashan - Such an address was quite natural from the herdsman of Tekoa. Bashan was famous for the fertility of its soil, and its flocks and herds; and the prophet here represents the iniquitous, opulent, idle, lazy drones, whether men or women, under the idea of fatted bullocks, which were shortly to be led out to the slaughter.
entries.d13f12bab33fc6072f0390f19e7db1100c4bd89e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34318" type="x-p"/> He will take you away with hooks - Two modes of fishing are here alluded to: <div eID="gen34318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34319" type="x-p"/> 1. Angling with rod, line, and baited hook. <div eID="gen34319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34320" type="x-p"/> 2. That with the gaff, eel-spear, harpoon, or such like; the first used in catching small fish, by which the common people may be here represented; the second, for catching large fish, such as leave the sea, and come up the rivers to deposit their spawn; or such as are caught in the sea, as sharks, whales, dolphins, and even the hippopotamus, to which the more powerful and opulent inhabitants may be likened. <div eID="gen34320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34321" type="x-p"/> But as the words in the text are generally feminine, it has been supposed that the prophecy is against the proud, powerful, voluptuous women. I rather think that the prophet speaks catachrestically; and means men of effeminate manners and idle lives. They are not the bulls of Bashan, but the cows; having little of the manly character remaining. Some understand the latter word as meaning a sort of basket or wicker fish-nets.
entries.ebe0efc1c6c66ad9d966ac7da3f2968d7587560f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34322" type="x-p"/> And ye shall go out at the breaches - Probably the metaphor is here kept up. They shall be caught by the hooks, or by the nets; and though they may make breaches in the latter by their flouncing when caught, they shall be taken out at these very breaches; and cast, not in the palace, but into a reservoir, to be kept awhile, and afterwards be taken out to be destroyed. Samaria itself is the net; your adversaries shall besiege it, and make breaches in its walls. At those breaches ye shall endeavor to make your escape, but ye shall be caught and led into captivity, where most of you shall be destroyed. See Houbigant on this passage.
entries.0d0e7c0139f6b721070b46e407df697e7d506100: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34323" type="x-p"/> Come to Beth-el and transgress - Spoken ironically. Go on to worship your calves at Beth-el; and multiply your transgressions at Gilgal; the very place where I rolled away the reproach of your fathers, by admitting them there into my covenant by circumcision. A place that should have ever been sacred to me; but you have now desecrated it by enormous idolatries. Let your morning and evening sacrifices be offered still to your senseless gods; and continue to support your present vicious priesthood by the regular triennial tithes which should have been employed in my service; and: -
entries.8e1d2d709de861412a8dfd67fb4d1dd54e8f96e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34324" type="x-p"/> Over a sacrifice of thanksgiving - To the senseless metal, and the unfeeling stock and stone images, from which ye never did, and never could receive any help. Proceed yet farther, and bring free-will offerings; testify superabundant gratitude to your wooden and metallic gods, to whom ye are under such immense imaginary obligations! Proclaim and publish these offerings, and set forth the perfections of the objects of your worship; and see what they can do for you, when I, Jehovah, shall send drought, and blasting, and famine, and pestilence, and the sword among you.
entries.5db2a3ec08b2820a6d12e5006a1f398096f74b6a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34325" type="x-p"/> Cleanness of teeth - Scarcity of bread, as immediately explained. Ye shall have no trouble in cleaning your teeth, for ye shall have nothing to eat. <div eID="gen34325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34326" type="x-p"/> Yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the Lord - This reprehension is repeated live times in this chapter; and in it are strongly implied God's longsuffering, his various modes of fatherly chastisement, the ingratitude of the people, and their obstinate wickedness. The famine mentioned here is supposed to be that which is spoken of <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.1">2Kgs 8:1</reference>; but it is most likely to have been that mentioned by Joel, chaps. 1 and 2.
entries.106708776dd1f0c374fd163367ff680dfff83220: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34327" type="x-p"/> When there were yet three months to the harvest - St. Jerome says, from the end of April, when the latter rain falls, until harvest, there are three months, May, June, and July, in which no rain falls in Judea. The rain, therefore, that God had withheld from them, was that which was usual in the spring months, particularly in April. <div eID="gen34327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34328" type="x-p"/> I caused it to rain upon one city - To prove to them that this rain did not come fortuitously or of necessity, God was pleased to make these most evident distinctions. One city had rain and could fill all its tanks or cisterns, while a neighboring city had none. One farm or field was well watered, and abundant in its crops, while one contiguous to it had not a shower. In these instances a particular providence was most evident. "And yet, they did not return to the Lord."
entries.1c4d538f5066369b7ee1bcfcb71fcafe18bd640a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34329" type="x-p"/> I have smitten you with blasting and mildew - He sent blasting and mildew on the crops, and the locust on the gardens, vineyards, and fields; and this in such a way as to show it was a Divine judgment. They saw this; "yet they did not return to the Lord!"
entries.3aae69e349ccddbe1023442e20478a8c2eb2366c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34330" type="x-p"/> I have sent - the pestilence - After the blasting and the mildew, the pestilence came; and it acted among them as one of the plagues of Egypt. Besides this, he had suffered their enemies to attack and prevail against them; alluding to the time in which the Syrians besieged Samaria, and reduced it to the most extreme necessity, when the head of an ass was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung for five; and mothers ate the flesh of their children that had died through hunger, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.25">2Kgs 6:25</reference>. And the people were miraculously relieved by the total slaughter of the Syrians by the unseen hand of God, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.1">2Kgs 7:1</reference>, etc. And yet, after all those signal judgments, and singular mercies, "they did not return unto the Lord!"
entries.bfb4ad69b4f433f70710ad8f90d8c53548b1a67a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34331" type="x-p"/> I have overthrown some of you - In the destruction of your cities I have shown my judgments as signally as I did in the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; and those of you that did escape were as "brands plucked out of the fire;" if not consumed, yet much scorched. And as the judgment was evidently from my hand, so was the deliverance; "and yet ye have not returned unto me, saith the Lord."
entries.5764d5849497a15be108bbe3cfdd0634e89c5e34: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34332" type="x-p"/> Therefore thus will I do unto thee - I will continue my judgments, I will fight against you; and, because I am thus determined: - <div eID="gen34332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34333" type="x-p"/> Prepare to meet thy God, O Israel - This is a military phrase, and is to be understood as a challenge to come out to battle. As if the Lord had said, I will attack you immediately. Throw yourselves into a posture of defense, summon your idols to your help: and try how far your strength, and that of your gods, will avail you against the unconquerable arm of the Lord of hosts! This verse has been often painfully misapplied by public teachers; it has no particular relation to the day of judgment, nor to the hour of death. These constructions are impositions on the text.
entries.07ec4e2ceea2f67c48afaa1059fc7bc493bea41e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34334" type="x-p"/> He that formeth the mountains - Here is a powerful description of the majesty of God. He formed the earth; he created the wind; he knows the inmost thoughts of the heart; he is the Creator of darkness and light; he steps from mountain to mountain, and has all things under his feet! Who is he who hath done and can do all these things? Jehovah Elohim Tsebaoth, that is his name. <div eID="gen34334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34335" type="x-p"/> 1. The self-existing, eternal, and independent Being. <div eID="gen34335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34336" type="x-p"/> 2. The God who is in covenant with mankind. <div eID="gen34336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34337" type="x-p"/> 3. The universal Commander of all the hosts of earth and heaven. This name is farther illustrated in the following chapter. These words are full of instruction, and may be a subject of profitable meditation to every serious mind.  <chapter eID="Amos.4"/> <div eID="gen34337" type="x-p"/>

entries.52c4d7ac1a94c8696766be9ec9b4500a76edc7da: <reference osisRef="Amos.4.1-Amos.4.3">Amo 4:1-3</reference> <hi type="italic">“Hear this word, ye cows of Bashan, that are upon the mountain of Samaria, that oppress there the humble and crush the poor, that say to their lords, Bring hither, that we may drink.</hi> Amo 4:2. <hi type="italic">The Lord Jehovah hath sworn by His holiness: behold, days come upon you, that they drag you away with hooks, and your last one with fish-hooks.</hi> Amo 4:3. <hi type="italic">And ye will go out through breaches in the wall, every one before him, and be cast away to Harmon, is the saying of Jehovah.” </hi> The commencement of this chapter is closely connected, so far as the contents are concerned, with the chapter immediately preceding. The prophet having there predicted, that when the kingdom was conquered by its enemies, the voluptuous grandees would perish, with the exception of a very few who would hardly succeed in saving their lives, turns now to the voluptuous women of Samaria, to predict in their case a shameful transportation into exile. The introduction, “Hear this word,” does not point therefore to a new prophecy, but simply to a fresh stage in the prophecy, so that we cannot even agree with Ewald in taking <reference osisRef="Amos.4.1-Amos.4.3">Amo 4:1-3</reference> as the conclusion of the previous prophecy (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.1-Amos.3.15">Amo 3:1-15</reference>). The cows of Bashan are well-fed, fat cows, βόες εὔτροφοι, <hi type="italic">vaccae pingues</hi> (Symm., Jer.), as Bashan had fat pastures, and for that reason the tribes that were richest in flocks and herds had asked for it as their inheritance (Numbers 32). The fuller definitions which follow show very clearly that by the cows of Bashan, Amos meant the rich, voluptuous, and violent inhabitants of Samaria. It is doubtful, however, whether he meant the rich and wanton wives of the great, as most of the modern commentators follow Theodor., Theodoret, and others, in assuming; or “the rulers of Israel, and all the leading men of the ten tribes, who spent their time in pleasure and robbery” (Jerome); or “those rich, luxurious, and lascivious inhabitants of the palace of whom he had spoken in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.9">Amo 3:9</reference>-10” (Maurer), as the Chald., Luther, Calvin, and others suppose, and whom he calls cows, not oxen, to denote their effeminacy and their unbridled licentiousness. In support of the latter opinion we might adduce not only Hos 10:11, where Ephraim is compared to a young heifer, but also the circumstance that from <reference osisRef="Amos.3.4">Amo 3:4</reference> onwards the prophecy refers to the Israelites as a whole. But neither of these arguments proves very much. The simile in Hos 10:11 applies to Ephraim as a kingdom of people, and the natural personification as a woman prepares the way for the comparison to an <hi type="italic">‛eglâh</hi>; whereas voluptuous and tyrannical grandees would be more likely to be compared to the bulls of Bashan (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.13">Psa 22:13</reference>). And so, again, the transition in Hos 10:4 to the Israelites as a whole furnishes no help in determining more precisely who are addressed in Hos 10:1-3. By the cows of Bashan, therefore, we understand the voluptuous women of Samaria, after the analogy of Isa 3:16. and <reference osisRef="Isa.32.9-Isa.32.13">Isa 32:9-13</reference>, more especially because it is only by forcing the last clause of <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Isa 32:1</reference> that it can be understood as referring to men. שׁמעוּ for שׁמענה, because the verb stands first (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.32.11">Isa 32:11</reference>). The mountain of Samaria is mentioned in the place of the city built upon the mountain (see at <reference osisRef="Amos.3.9">Amo 3:9</reference>). The sin of these women consisted in the tyrannical oppression of the poor, whilst they asked their lords, i.e., their husbands, to procure them the means of debauchery. For עשׁק and רצץ, compare <reference osisRef="Deut.28.33">Deu 28:33</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.3-1Sam.12.4">1Sa 12:3-4</reference>, where the two words are already connected. הביאה stands in the singular, because every wife speaks in this way to her husband. <div eID="gen16376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16377" type="x-p"/> The announcement of the punishment for such conduct is introduced with a solemn oath, to make an impression, if possible, upon the hardened hearts. Jehovah swears by His holiness, i.e., as the Holy One, who cannot tolerate unrighteousness. כּי (for) before הנּה introduces the oath. Hitzig takes ונשּׂא as a <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, as in the similar formula in 2Ki 20:17; but he takes it as a passive used impersonally with an accusative, after <reference osisRef="Gen.35.26">Gen 35:26</reference> and other passages (though not <reference osisRef="Exod.13.7">Exo 13:7</reference>). But as נשּׂא unquestionably occurs as a <hi type="italic">piel</hi> in 1Ki 9:11, it is more natural to take the same form as a <hi type="italic">piel</hi> in this instance also, and whilst interpreting it impersonally, to think of the enemy as understood. <hi type="italic">Tsinnōth</hi> = <hi type="italic">tsinnı̄m</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.5">Pro 22:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.5.5">Job 5:5</reference>, צנּה = צּן, thorns, hence hooks; so also <hi type="italic">sı̄rōth</hi> = <hi type="italic">sı̄rı̄m</hi>, thorns, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.13">Isa 34:13</reference>; Hos 2:8. <hi type="italic">Dūgâh</hi>, fishery; hence <hi type="italic">sı̄rōth dūgâh</hi>, fish-hooks. <hi type="italic">'Achărı̄th</hi> does not mean posterity, or the young brood that has grown up under the instruction and example of the parents (Hitzig), but simply “the <hi type="italic">end</hi>,” the opposite of <hi type="italic">rē'shı̄th</hi>, the beginning. It is “end,” however, in different senses. Here it signifies the remnant (Chaldee), i.e., those who remain and are not dragged away with <hi type="italic">tsinnōth</hi>; so that the thought expressed is “all, even to the very last” (compare Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Christology</hi>, i. p. 368). אחריתכן has a feminine suffix, whereas masculine suffixes were used before (אתכם, עליכם); the universal gender, out of which the feminine was first formed. The figure is not taken from animals, into whose noses hooks and rings are inserted to tame them, or from large fishes that are let down into the water again by nose-hooks; for the technical terms applied to these hooks are חח, חוח, and חכּה (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.4">Eze 29:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.41.1-Job.41.2">Job 41:1-2</reference>); but from the catching of fishes, that are drawn out of the fish-pond with hooks. Thus shall the voluptuous, wanton women be violently torn away or carried off from the midst of the superfluity and debauchery in which they lived as in their proper element. פּרצים תּצאנה, to go out of rents in the wall, יצא being construed, as it frequently is, with the accusative of the place; we should say, “though rents in the wall,” i.e., through breaches made in the wall at the taking of the city, not out at the gates, because they had been destroyed or choked up with rubbish at the storming of the city. “Every one before her,” i.e., without looking round to the right or to the left (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.6.5">Jos 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.20">Jos 6:20</reference>). The words והשּׁלכתּנה ההרמונה are difficult, on account of the ἁπ. λεγ. ההרמונה, and have not yet been satisfactorily explained. The form השׁלכתּנה for השׁלכתּן is probably chosen simply for the purpose of obtaining a resemblance in sound to תּצאנה, and is sustained by אתּנה for אתּן in <reference osisRef="Gen.31.6">Gen 31:6</reference> and Eze 13:11. השׁליך is applied to thrusting into exile, as in Deu 29:27. <div eID="gen16377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16378" type="x-p"/> The ἁπ. λεγ. ההרמונה with ה htiw  <hi type="italic">loc.</hi> appears to indicate the place to which they were to be carried away or cast out. But the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> השׁלכתּנה does not suit this, and consequently nearly all the earlier translators have rendered it as a passive, ἀποῤῥι-φήσεσθε (lxx), <hi type="italic">projiciemini</hi> (Jerome); so also the Syr. and Chald. ויגלון יתהון, “men will carry them away captive.” One Hebrew codex actually gives the <hi type="italic">hophal</hi>. And to this reading we must adhere; for the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> furnishes no sense at all, since the intransitive or reflective meaning, to plunge, or cast one’s self, cannot be sustained, and is not supported at all by the passages quoted by Hitzig, viz., 2Ki 10:25 and <reference osisRef="Job.27.22">Job 27:22</reference>; and still less does <hi type="italic">haharmōnâh</hi> denote the object cast away by the women when they go into captivity.<note placement="foot">The Masoretic pointing probably originated in the idea that <hi type="italic">harmōnâh</hi>, corresponding to the talmudic <hi type="italic">harmânâ'</hi>, signifies royal power or dominion, and so Rashi interprets it: “ye will cast away the authority, i.e., the almost regal authority, or that pride and arrogance with which you bear yourselves to-day” (Ros.). This explanation would be admissible, if it were not that the use of a word which never occurs again in the old Hebrew for a thing so frequently mentioned in the Old Testament, rendered it very improbable. At any rate, it is more admissible than the different conjectures of the most recent commentators. Thus Hitzig, for example (<hi type="italic">Comm</hi>. ed. 3), would resolve <hi type="italic">haharmōnâh</hi> into <hi type="italic">hâhâr</hi> and <hi type="italic">mōnâh</hi> = <hi type="italic">meōnâh</hi> (“and ye will plunge headlong to the mountain as a place of refuge”). The objections to this are, (1) that <hi type="italic">hishlı̄kh</hi> does not mean to plunge headlong; (2) the improbability of <hi type="italic">meōnâh</hi> being contracted into <hi type="italic">mōnâh</hi>, when Amos has <hi type="italic">meōnâh</hi> in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.4">Amo 3:4</reference>; and lastly, the fact that <hi type="italic">meōnâh</hi> means simply a dwelling, not a place of refuge. Ewald would read <hi type="italic">hâhâr rimmōnâh</hi> after the lxx, and renders it, “ye will cast Rimmonah to the mountain,” understanding by Rimmonah a female deity of the Syrians. But antiquity knows nothing of any such female deity; and from the reference to a deity called <hi type="italic">Rimmon</hi> in 2Ki 5:18, you cannot possibly infer the existence of a goddess <hi type="italic">Rimmonah</hi>. The explanation given by Schlottmann (<hi type="italic">Hiob</hi>, p. 132) and Paul Bötticher (<hi type="italic">Rudimenta mythologiae semit.</hi> 1848, p. 10) - namely, that <hi type="italic">harmōnâh</hi> as the Phoenician goddess <hi type="italic">Chusarthis</hi>, called by the Greeks Ἁρμονία - is still more untenable, since Ἁρμονία is no more derived from the talmudic <hi type="italic">harmân</hi> than this is from the Sanscrit <hi type="italic">pramāna</hi> (Bötticher, l.c. p. 40); on the contrary, <hi type="italic">harmân</hi> signifies loftiness, from the Semitic root הרם, to be high, and it cannot be shown that there was a goddess called <hi type="italic">Harman</hi> or <hi type="italic">Harmonia</hi> in the Phoenician worship. Lastly, the fanciful idea of Bötticher, that <hi type="italic">harmōnâh</hi> is contracted from <hi type="italic">hâhar rimmōnâh</hi>, and that the meaning is, “and then ye throw, i.e., remove, the mountain (your Samaria) to Rimmon, that ancient place of refuge for expelled tribes” (Jdg 20:45.), needs no refutation.</note> <div eID="gen16378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16379" type="x-p"/> The literal meaning of <hi type="italic">harmōnâh</hi> or <hi type="italic">harmōn</hi> still remains uncertain. According to the etymology of הרם, to be high, it apparently denotes a high land: at the same time, it can neither be taken as an appellative, as Hesselberg and Maurer suppose, “the high land;” nor in the sense of <hi type="italic">'armōn</hi>, a citadel or palace, as Kimchi and Gesenius maintain. The former interpretation is open to the objection, that we cannot possibly imagine why Amos should have formed a word of his own, and one which never occurs again in the Hebrew language, to express the simple idea of a mountain or high land; and the second to this objection, that “the citadel” would require something to designate it as a citadel or fortress in the land of the enemy. The unusual word certainly points to the name of a land or district, though we have no means of determining it more precisely.<note placement="foot">Even the early translators have simply rendered <hi type="italic">haharmōnâh</hi> according to the most uncertain conjectures. Thus lxx, εἰς τὸὄρος τὸ Ῥομμάν (<hi type="italic">al.</hi> Ῥεμμάν); Aq., <hi type="italic">mons Armona</hi>; Theod., <hi type="italic">mons Mona</hi>; the <hi type="italic">Quinta: excelsus mons</hi> (according to Jerome); and Theodoret attributes to Theodot. ὑψηλὸν ὄρος. The Chaldee paraphrases it thus: להלאה מן טוּרי הרמיני, “far beyond the mountains of Armenia.” Symmachus also had <hi type="italic">Armenia</hi>, according to the statement of Theodoret and Jerome. But this explanation is probably merely an inference drawn from 2Ki 17:23, and cannot be justified, as Bochart supposes, on the ground that <hi type="italic">mōnâh</hi> or <hi type="italic">mōn</hi> is identical with <hi type="italic">minnı̄</hi>.</note>
entries.8ccdba4bd853abcadc697c3cfd1cb87e2fd2bb9d: <reference osisRef="Amos.4.4-Amos.4.5">Amo 4:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen16379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16380" type="x-p"/> After this threat directed against the voluptuous women of the capital, the prophecy turns again to all the people. In bitter irony, Amos tells them to go on with zeal in their idolatrous sacrifices, and to multiply their sin. But they will not keep back the divine judgment by so doing. Amo 4:4. <hi type="italic">“Go to Bethel, and sin; to Gilgal, multiply sinning; and offer your slain-offerings in the morning, your tithes every three days.</hi> Amo 4:5. <hi type="italic">And kindle praise-offerings of that which is leavened, and cry out freewill-offerings, proclaim it; for so ye love it, O sons of Israel, is the saying of the Lord, of Jehovah.” </hi>“Amos here describes how zealously the people of Israel went on pilgrimage to Bethel, and Gilgal, and Beersheba, those places of sacred associations; with what superabundant diligence they offered sacrifice and paid tithes; who they would rather do too much than too little, so that they even burnt upon the altar a portion of the leavened loaves of the praise-offering, which were only intended for the sacrificial meals, although none but unleavened bread was allowed to be offered; and lastly, how in their pure zeal for multiplying the works of piety, they so completely mistook their nature, as to summon by a public proclamation to the presentation of freewill-offerings, the very peculiarity of which consisted in the fact that they had no other prompting than the will of the offerer” (v. Hofmann, <hi type="italic">Schriftbeweis</hi>, ii. 2, p. 373). The irony of the summons to maintain their worship comes out very distinctly in the words וּפשׁעוּ, and sin, or fall away from God. הגּלגּל is not a nominative absolute, “as for Gilgal,” but an accusative, and בּאוּ is to be repeated from the first clause. The absence of the copula before הרבּוּ does not compel us to reject the Masoretic accentuation, and connect הגּלגּל with פּלשׁעוּ, as Hitzig does, so as to obtain the unnatural thought, “sin ye towards Gilgal.” On Gilgal mentioned along with Bethel as a place of idolatrous worship (here and <reference osisRef="Amos.5.5">Amo 5:5</reference>, as in Hos 4:15; Hos 9:15, and Hos 12:12), see at Hos 4:15. Offer your slain-offerings <hi type="italic">labbōqer</hi>, for the morning, i.e., every morning, like <hi type="italic">layyōm</hi> in Jer 37:21. This is required by the parallel <hi type="italic">lishlōsheth yâmı̄m</hi>, on the three of days, i.e., every three days. זבחים ... הביאוּ does not refer to the morning sacrifice prescribed in the law (Num 28:3) - for that is always called <hi type="italic">‛ōlâh</hi>, not <hi type="italic">zebach</hi> - but to slain sacrifices that were offered every morning, although the offering of <hi type="italic">zebhâchı̄m</hi> every morning presupposes the presentation of the daily morning burnt-offering. What is said concerning the tithe rests upon the Mosaic law of the second tithe, which was to be brought every three years (<reference osisRef="Deut.14.28">Deu 14:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.26.12">Deu 26:12</reference>; compare my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archäol.</hi> §71, Anm. 7). The two clauses, however, are not to be understood as implying that the Israelites had offered slain sacrifices every morning, and tithe every three days. Amos is speaking hyperbolically, to depict the great zeal displayed in their worship; and the thought is simply this: “If ye would offer slain sacrifices every morning, and tithe every three days, ye would only thereby increase your apostasy from the living God.” The words, “kindle praise-offerings of that which is leavened,” have been misinterpreted in various ways. קטּר, an <hi type="italic">inf. absol.</hi> used instead of the <hi type="italic">imperative</hi> (see Ges. §131, 4, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). According to <reference osisRef="Lev.7.12-Lev.7.14">Lev 7:12-14</reference>, the praise-offering (<hi type="italic">tōdâh</hi>) was to consist not only of unleavened cakes and pancakes with oil poured upon them, but also of cakes of leavened bread. The latter, however, were not to be placed upon the altar, but one of them was to be assigned to the priest who sprinkled the blood, and the rest to be eaten at the sacrificial meal. Amos now charges the people with having offered that which was leavened instead of unleavened cakes and pancakes, and with having burned it upon the altar, contrary to the express prohibition of the law in Lev 2:11. His words are not to be understood as signifying that, although outwardly the praise-offerings consisted of that which was unleavened, according to the command of the law, yet inwardly they were so base that they resembled unleavened cakes, inasmuch as whilst the material of the leaven was absent, the true nature of the leaven - namely, malice and wickedness - was there in all the greater quantity (Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Dissertations</hi>, vol. i. p. 143 translation). The meaning is rather this, that they were not content with burning upon the altar unleavened cakes made from the materials provided for the sacrifice, but that they burned some of the leavened loaves as well, in order to offer as much as possible to God. What follows answers to this: call out <hi type="italic">nedâbhōth</hi>, i.e., call out that men are to present freewill-offerings. The emphasis is laid upon קראוּ, which is therefore still further strengthened by השׁמעוּ. Their calling out <hi type="italic">nedâbhōth</hi>, i.e., their ordering freewill-offerings to be presented, was an exaggerated act of zeal, inasmuch as the sacrifices which ought to have been brought out of purely spontaneous impulse (cf. Lev 22:18.; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.6">Deu 12:6</reference>), were turned into a matter of moral compulsion, or rather of legal command. The words, “for so ye love it,” show how this zeal in the worship lay at the heart of the nation. It is also evident from the whole account, that the worship in the kingdom of the ten tribes was conducted generally according to the precepts of the Mosaic law. <div eID="gen16380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16381" type="x-p"/> But as Israel would not desist from its idolatrous worship, Jehovah would also continue to visit the people with judgments, as He had already done, though without effecting any conversion to their God. This last thought is explained in <reference osisRef="Amos.4.6-Amos.4.11">Amo 4:6-11</reference> in a series of instances, in which the expression ולא שׁבתּם עדי (and ye have not returned to me), which is repeated five times, depicts in the most thorough manner the unwearied love of the Lord to His rebellious children.
entries.e3f4dd4911a2fce3392d71159c34df9313bf0a59: <reference osisRef="Amos.4.6">Amo 4:6</reference> <hi type="italic">“And I have also given you cleanness of teeth in all your towns, and want of bread in all your places: and ye have not returned to me, is the saying of Jehovah.” </hi> The strongly adversative וגם אני forms the antithesis to כן אהבתּם: Ye love to persist in your idolatry, and yet I have tried all means of turning you to me. Cleanness of teeth is explained by the parallel “want of bread.” The first chastisement, therefore, consisted in famine, with which God visited the nation, as He had threatened the transgressors that He would do in the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.48">Deu 28:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.57">Deu 28:57</reference>). For שׁוּב עד, compare Hos 14:2.
entries.92b11736b871c32ba5fbc2b0635f131ec3f28055: <reference osisRef="Amos.4.7-Amos.4.8">Amo 4:7-8</reference> <hi type="italic">“And I have also withholden the rain from you, in yet three months to the harvest; and have caused it to rain upon one city, and I do not cause it to rain upon another. One field is rained upon, and the field upon which it does not rain withers.</hi> Amo 4:8. <hi type="italic">And two, three towns stagger to one town to drink water, and are not satisfied: and ye have not returned to me, is the saying of Jehovah.” </hi> The second punishment mentioned is the withholding of rain, or drought, which was followed by the failure of the harvest and the scarcity of water (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.19-Lev.26.20">Lev 26:19-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.23">Deu 28:23</reference>).
